book.title: Make It Stick
book.author: Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III, Mark A. McDaniel

confidence_note: The surgical residents study is in ch. 3 and matches Moulton et al., Annals of Surgery 2006. The '16 percent' figure is as stated in the book (not in the abstract). Anki, a fixed 3-day/1-week/1-month schedule and the quoted line in the old text are not in the book and are dropped.
facts: Thirty-eight surgical residents took four short lessons in microsurgery: how to reattach tiny vessels, each lesson instruction plus practice.
Half did all four lessons in one day, the normal in-service schedule; the other half had a week between lessons.
A month after the last session, the spaced group did better on every measure: time to finish, number of hand movements, and success reattaching the severed, pulsating aortas of live rats.
Among the one-day group, 16 percent damaged the rats' vessels beyond repair and could not complete the surgery.
The findings prompted the medical school to reexamine its habit of cramming a technique into one intensive session.
The authors' explanation: consolidation takes hours or days; the extra effort of retrieving after 'a little forgetting' retriggers it.
How long to wait: long enough that practice isn't mindless repetition and a little forgetting has set in, not so long that it becomes relearning.
Spaced practice feels less productive; even people who did better with spacing believed they had learned more from massed practice.
scene_details: four short lessons in reattaching tiny vessels
the severed, pulsating aorta of a live rat
the normal in-service schedule: all in one day
tension: Same lessons, same total time, but one schedule produced surgeons who damaged vessels beyond repair.
opening_idea: Start with the rat's aorta and the residents who could not finish the repair, without saying yet which group they were in.

lessons.idea: Let a little forgetting happen before you practice again, because the effort of recalling is what fixes the skill.
lessons.anchor: Week-apart lessons beat one-day lessons a month later.

reflect_final: Which skill would you practice differently this month if you planned the gaps between sessions as deliberately as the sessions?

use_cases.situation: Planning onboarding for a new process
use_cases.move: In a surgical study, lessons a week apart beat the same lessons in one day. Can we split the training into four short sessions?

use_cases.situation: Child wants to practise piano for two hours on Sunday only
use_cases.move: Suggest short sessions on several days and let them notice what they still remember each time.
Put cards you miss back in the first pile and wait a day before the next round.

pocket_idea: Wait until a skill has slipped a little, then practise; the struggle to recall is the lesson.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Surgeons who learned in one day were the ones who damaged the rats' vessels beyond repair.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: 38 residents, four microsurgery lessons; half in one day, half a week apart. A month later the spaced group was faster, used fewer movements, and succeeded more; 16% of the one-day group couldn't finish. A little forgetting makes recall work.
